edges.description: Diffuse pan-uveal cytokine signaling and endothelial activation drive leukocyte recruitment across blood-ocular barriers into all compartments.
Inflammation spanning the iris, ciliary body, and choroid directly manifests clinically as panuveitis.
Diffuse intraocular inflammation disrupts ocular transparency and retinal function.
Anterior-segment iris and ciliary body inflammation within panuveitis triggers light-evoked ciliary spasm and photophobia.
Inflammatory involvement of the iris and ciliary body within panuveitis causes ocular pain.
Spillover of inflammatory cells and exudates into the vitreous cavity causes vitreous opacities perceived as floaters.
Cellular infiltration and inflammatory exudation across compromised blood-retinal barriers promote macular edema.
Severe chorioretinal inflammation and subretinal exudation or vitreoretinal traction lead to serous or tractional retinal detachment.
Chronic intraocular compartment inflammation (along with corticosteroid exposure in treated patients) accelerates lens opacification.
Chronic intraocular inflammation (as well as corticosteroid-induced ocular hypertension in treated patients) impairs aqueous humor outflow and elevates intraocular pressure, causing uveitic glaucoma.
Posterior-segment inflammatory infiltration, papillitis, and elevated intraocular pressure contribute to optic nerve injury.
Infectious or systemic immune-mediated triggers initiate pan-uveal intraocular inflammation.
Altered HLA ocular peptide presentation, Th17 pathway genetic susceptibility, and disinhibited NF-kappaB signaling lower activation thresholds and promote pan-uveal inflammation.

nodes.description: Polymorphisms in MHC class I and II molecules (such as HLA-B*51 and HLA-B27) alter ocular peptide presentation to T lymphocytes, while susceptibility variants in the Th17-pathway receptor IL23R and haploinsufficiency of the NF-kappaB negative regulator TNFAIP3 (A20) dysregulate adaptive and innate immune signaling, lowering activation thresholds for intraocular autoimmunity.

biological_processes: antigen processing and presentation of peptide antigen via MHC class I

evidence.snippet: As outlined above, HLA polymorphisms shape which ocular peptides are displayed to T-cells and modify risk; prominent examples include HLA-B27 with acute anterior uveitis, HLA-A29 with birdshot chorioretinopathy, and HLA-B*51 with Behçet’s disease (Table 2) (221).
For example, IL23R is a key genetic component of Th17 signalling and is implicated in the pathophysiology of Behçet’s and Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease (223).

Additional immune-regulatory loci-STAT4, CCR1, IRF8, TNFAIP3 (A20)-have been linked in cohort- and disease-specific analyses. A20 haploinsufficiency, which normally acts as a brake on the NF-κB inflammation pathway, disinhibits NF-κB signalling, lowering activation thresholds for ocular autoimmunity (221, 224).

nodes.description: Panuveitis can arise from infectious causes, idiopathic inflammation, or systemic immune-mediated disease. Etiologic classification is clinically central because antimicrobial therapy is required for infectious disease, whereas noninfectious disease often requires corticosteroids and steroid-sparing immunosuppression.

evidence.snippet: Uveitis is classified as noninfectious or infectious
37% to 49% are associated with systemic disease

nodes.description: Intravitreal corticosteroid injections or sustained-release implants (such as dexamethasone or triamcinolone) provide targeted posterior-segment and pan-uveal anti-inflammatory control in moderate to severe noninfectious panuveitis, though local corticosteroid delivery carries elevated risks of cataract progression and corticosteroid-induced glaucoma.

evidence.snippet: require systemic and/or intravitreal corticosteroids and immunosuppressive agents.

nodes.description: Methotrexate is a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug used as a steroid-sparing treatment option for posterior-segment noninfectious uveitis that can include panuveitis.
